title: The tables go over (Matthew 21:12–13)
hook: in the temple courts he overturns the money changers' tables

segments.voice: Yesterday, hosanna: save, please, shouted for a king on a donkey, and the stones would cry out. Today the gentle king walks into the temple, and things get loud.

Children taken up in his arms. Hands on the sick. A king on a donkey. And then this. The temple in Jerusalem, days before Passover: the center of Jewish worship, packed with pilgrims from everywhere. The outer court, a huge open space, is full of stalls: people selling doves and animals for the sacrifices, money changers at their tables. Noise, bargaining, animals, crowds. And Jesus walks in.
screen: `CHILDREN, THE SICK, A DONKEY.` → `THE TEMPLE BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `STALLS, COINS AND DOVES.`

segments.voice: Matthew tells it fast, in the King James Bible: "And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves." Coins spilling across the stones. Birds flapping. Then he explains, quoting two prophets at once: "It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves." The first half is from Isaiah; Mark gives the full line: a house of prayer for all nations. The second half is from Jeremiah, who stood in the gate of the temple of his own day and warned people not to treat God's house as a den, a hideout. So this isn't an attack on the temple, or on Judaism. It's a Jewish prophet in the line of Isaiah and Jeremiah, calling the temple back to what it was for. The selling itself served a purpose: pilgrims from far away needed doves and animals to offer, and someone to change their money. But some readers point out that the stalls likely stood in the outer court, where people who weren't Jewish could come and pray. If that court is a market, where do they go? All four Gospels tell this story; John puts it near the start of Jesus's work, and adds a whip of cords. And look at what Matthew says happens right after the tables go over. The blind and the lame come to him in the temple, and he heals them, and children start shouting hosanna. The noise of trade gives way to the noise of healing and praise.
screen: `HE OVERTHREW THE TABLES.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `A PROPHET LIKE JEREMIAH.` · `THEN THE BLIND AND THE LAME COME.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Think of one cluttered corner in your life: a desk, a shelf, a car seat, a phone's home screen, or a crowded hour with no room left in it. Picture it clear, with room to breathe, room to think, room to pray if you pray. You don't have to clear it all; just choose the one small table you'd turn over first.
Moneychangers. The traders Jesus found at their tables in the temple's outer court, and sent scattering so the court could be, again, a house of prayer.
Your line: make room for prayer. Tomorrow, a supper in Bethany, and a jar of perfume. See you then.

howItsDone: Many churches read the cleansing of the temple in Lent or Holy Week. Christians often turn to it when thinking about keeping places of worship for prayer, and about money and faith.

original.note: Greek: a money changer, from kollybos, a small coin or the fee for changing money.

what it means: a prophet calls the temple back to its purpose, a house of prayer, and clears room for the blind, the lame and the children.

chat.says: Was Jesus attacking the temple when he flipped over those tables?
options: No. Like Isaiah and Jeremiah, he was calling it back to being a house of prayer.
No. He was protesting the Roman soldiers who stood guard in the temple courts.
Yes. He was clearing the court so his own followers could meet there instead.
chat.meaning: He quoted Isaiah and Jeremiah: my house shall be called the house of prayer. A Jewish prophet, calling the temple back to what it was for.

moneychangers.meaning: traders who changed pilgrims' money at tables in the temple

outer court.meaning: the temple's huge open space, where non-Jews could come and pray

Isaiah.meaning: prophet who called the temple a house of prayer for all nations

Jeremiah.meaning: prophet who warned against treating God's house as a den

notes: Money changers and the temple tax in Tyrian coinage; sale of sacrificial animals for pilgrims. Commonly stated; confirm.
Location in the Court of the Gentiles is a common scholarly view but not stated in the text ('many scholars think').
The script frames Jesus as a Jewish prophet in the line of Isaiah and Jeremiah and explicitly avoids framing this as an attack on Judaism. Confirm tone.
Mark 11:17 has 'of all nations'; Matthew does not. The script attributes the fuller line to Mark.
John 2:13–17 places the event early and includes the whip of cords.

Fresh review (days 57–74): fixed an error, Jeremiah did not stand 'in this same temple' (his was the first temple, Herod's the second); now 'the temple of his own day' (Jeremiah 7:2). Hook drops 'Most of us picture' and 'the holiest place in the Jewish world'; the Court of the Gentiles and the temple-tax coinage are no longer stated as fact.
